domains.summary: Leadership under pressure: incident command, decision-making with incomplete information, and blameless learning. General educational material; confers no certificate and implies no endorsement.

scenarios.title: Who takes command
scenarios.situation: The checkout service is down. Priya, your best debugger, is already deep in the logs. You are the on-call lead. Someone needs to coordinate: paging, status updates, and stakeholder calls.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right staffing decision?
choices: You take the incident commander role and let Priya keep debugging uninterrupted
Priya takes command since she knows the system best
You both debug together and skip formal roles to move faster
Wait for a manager to wake up and decide who is in charge
scenarios.why: The incident commander's job is coordination, not fixing: they run the clock, the comms, and the decision log while technical responders work. Putting your best debugger in the coordinator seat wastes your scarcest resource, and skipping roles guarantees dropped tasks like status updates.
scenarios.hint: Which job suffers more from interruption: debugging or coordinating?

scenarios.title: The first five minutes
scenarios.situation: Alerts fire: the API error rate jumped from 0.1% to 35% two minutes ago. Customers are noticing. Three engineers are in the channel asking what to do.
scenarios.prompt: What should happen in the first five minutes?
choices: Declare the incident, assign an incident commander, page the service owners, and post a first status update with a next-update time
Immediately roll back the last deploy, since it is probably the cause
Have everyone investigate in parallel and reconvene when someone finds the cause
Post in the company-wide channel asking if anyone else sees the problem
scenarios.why: Structure first, diagnosis second. Declaring the incident and assigning roles converts chaos into parallel work: responders investigate while the commander handles comms and the clock. Rolling back blind can destroy evidence or worsen things, and unstructured parallel investigation duplicates effort.
scenarios.hint: What turns three confused engineers into a team?

scenarios.title: Conflicting signals
scenarios.situation: During an outage, the dashboard shows database CPU at 95%, but the database specialist insists 'the DB is fine, it is always hot.' Two responders want to fail over the database now; the specialist wants to keep looking at the app tier.
scenarios.prompt: How should the incident commander resolve this?
choices: Trust the instrumented data over opinion: treat the database as the prime suspect while time-boxing a quick app-tier check
Defer to the specialist's experience and focus the team on the app tier
Fail over the database immediately to show decisive leadership
Let the team vote on which theory to pursue
scenarios.why: In incidents, measured data outranks seniority and gut feel: p99 query latency 50x over baseline is a fact, 'always hot' is a story. The commander arbitrates by evidence, keeps one primary theory with a time-boxed check of the alternative, and avoids both blind deference and impulsive failover.
scenarios.hint: Which input is a measurement and which is a memory?

scenarios.title: Just restart it
scenarios.situation: A VP joins the incident bridge 20 minutes in and says: 'Just restart the whole cluster, that fixed it last time.' The responders have a promising lead: a config change that correlates exactly with the error spike, and they need ten more minutes to confirm.
scenarios.prompt: What should the incident commander do?
choices: Acknowledge the VP, explain the team has a time-boxed lead, and commit to the restart as the fallback if the lead fails
Restart immediately; seniority decides in a crisis
Mute the VP and continue; incident bridges are no place for executives
Restart half the cluster as a compromise
scenarios.why: The commander's job includes managing stakeholders, not just the technical response. Acknowledging the suggestion, converting it into a planned fallback, and protecting the time-boxed investigation gets you the best of both: the team's lead is tested, and if it fails you already have an agreed next step. A blind restart destroys diagnostic state.
scenarios.hint: How do you honor the suggestion without obeying it blindly?

scenarios.title: Two fires at once
scenarios.situation: At 02:10 the payment service degrades. At 02:25, while that incident is still open, the authentication service starts failing too. You have one incident commander, six responders, and both services are customer-facing.
choices: Split into two incidents with two commanders, triage which is more severe, and staff the higher-severity one first with a skeleton crew on the other
Keep one incident and one commander covering both to avoid confusion
Pause the payments incident and move everyone to auth, since auth affects more users
Handle payments first to completion, then start on auth
scenarios.why: One commander cannot run two clocks, two comms streams, and two decision logs. Splitting creates clear ownership per incident, and explicit triage (severity first, then staffing) beats both serial handling and pretending one brain can track two fires. The lower-severity incident gets a holding pattern, not abandonment.
scenarios.hint: What breaks first when one person commands two incidents?

scenarios.title: The postmortem with a name on it
scenarios.situation: The outage review shows the root trigger clearly: an engineer ran a migration against the production database instead of staging. The timeline is documented. The team is waiting to see how leadership reacts.
scenarios.prompt: How should the postmortem handle the human error?
choices: Keep the review blameless: document what made the mistake easy (identical prompts, no guardrails) and fix the system with safeguards and owners
Name the engineer in the report so accountability is clear
Remove the human-error detail from the report to protect the engineer
Require the engineer to present the postmortem alone as a learning exercise
scenarios.why: Blameless does not mean accountless: it means the fix targets the system that allowed the error, not the person who made it. Punishing individuals teaches everyone to hide mistakes, which destroys the incident data you need. Documenting enabling conditions (identical prompts, missing confirmations) produces safeguards that prevent the whole class of error.
scenarios.hint: After this review, will the next person report their mistake faster or slower?

lessons.title: Command — Core concepts
concepts: The incident commander coordinates; they do not fix. Their products are the decision log, the comms cadence, and the staffing plan, while responders work the problem.
Declare early and structure fast: naming the incident, assigning roles, and setting the next-update time converts a crowd into a team in the first five minutes.
Decide by evidence under uncertainty: instrumented data outranks opinion and seniority; time-box competing theories instead of debating them.
Manage the bridge, not just the bug: stakeholders need scheduled updates and a say in fallbacks, not a front-row seat to raw debugging.
Span of control is real: one commander runs one incident; split command rather than splitting attention when fires multiply.
Learn blamelessly: postmortems fix the system conditions that made the error easy, because punishing people teaches hiding, and hiding kills your data.

example.code:
log() { printf '%s %s\n' "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" "$*" >> incident.log; }
log "INC-2041 declared - IC: Rivera"
log "Status page updated; next update in 15 min"
log "Theory A time-boxed to 10 min; fallback: restart cluster"
example.walkthrough: A decision log is the commander's cheapest superpower: timestamped lines turn a chaotic bridge into a reviewable record. Future you, the postmortem, and the auditors all read this file.

pitfalls: Common trap: the commander also debugging, which means nobody is running the clock or the comms.
Common trap: skipping the postmortem when the fix was easy; easy fixes hide systemic causes.
Common trap: vague status updates ('we're working on it') that force every stakeholder to ask for details individually.
Common trap: debating theories instead of time-boxing them; investigation needs a budget, not a winner.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Run a simulated incident timeline
labs.objective: Practice the commander's first 30 minutes: declaration, roles, comms cadence, and a decision log.
steps: Define the log() function above and create incident.log.
Declare INC-9001 at T+0 and assign yourself incident commander.
Log a status update every 5 simulated minutes with the current theory and next step.
Introduce one complication at T+15 (a stakeholder demanding an ETA) and log how you handled it.
Declare resolution at T+30 with the verified fix, then review the log for gaps.

checks.hint: Your log should open with the incident declaration line.
Count log lines: declaration plus updates should show a steady cadence.

labs.title: Write a blameless postmortem
labs.objective: Convert a simulated incident timeline into a postmortem with systemic action items.
steps: Create postmortem.md with sections: Summary, Timeline, Root causes, Action items.
Write the timeline from incident.log without naming individuals as causes.
For each cause, ask 'why' twice to reach a system condition, not a person.
Write each action item with an owner and a due date; no ownerless items.
Add one safeguard that would have made the triggering mistake hard to make.

checks.hint: Confirm the action-items section exists with owners and dates.

simulations.title: The 3 AM page
simulations.brief: 3:07 AM. Your phone is screaming: checkout is down, error rate 100%. You are the incident commander. The next ten minutes set the tone for the next ten hours.

steps.symptom: Checkout is fully down. Three engineers are awake in the channel, all talking at once, nobody leading.
evidence:
03:07 — checkout error rate 100% | revenue impact: ~$40k/hour
Channel: 3 engineers online, no IC declared, parallel theories flying
options: Start debugging immediately — every minute costs money
Declare yourself incident commander, open a dedicated channel, and assign roles: one debugger, one comms, one scribe
Wait for the VP to wake up and decide
Tell everyone to stay calm and go back to sleep while you look
steps.explain: The first job is not the fix — it is the structure. An IC, a channel, and three roles (debug, comms, scribe) turn chaos into a team. Debugging before declaring means five people stepping on each other's theories.

steps.symptom: Structure is up. The debugger thinks it is the database; the comms lead wants to post a status update saying 'we are investigating.'
evidence:
Debugger: 'DB connections spiking, I think it's the primary.'
Comms: 'Can I post that we're investigating?' | Scribe: logging
options: Post the update and let the debugger keep digging alone
Approve a factual status ('checkout is down, we are investigating, next update in 30 min'), and ask the debugger for evidence before acting on the DB theory
Fail over the database now — the theory sounds right
Tell comms to say nothing until there is a fix
steps.explain: Comms cadence is set early: factual, no speculation, next update promised. And theories need evidence before they become actions — failing over a database on a hunch can turn one outage into two.

steps.symptom: Root cause found: a deploy at 02:40 shipped a bad migration. Rollback is ready but the deploy's author is the debugger — and looks shattered.
evidence:
Cause: deploy 02:40, bad migration | Fix: rollback staged, tested
Debugger (deploy author): 'This is my fault. I'm so sorry.'
options: Execute the rollback, thank the debugger for finding it fast, and say the postmortem will focus on the system, not the person
Execute the rollback and reassign the debugger — they are compromised
Delay the rollback until the author is calmer
Announce in the channel that the debugger caused it so everyone knows
steps.explain: Fix first, humanity always. The rollback is the priority; the debugger who found their own bug fast is an asset, not a liability. And you say out loud, now, that the postmortem will be blameless — psychological safety is built in moments like this.

simulations.debrief: You built structure before chasing the fix, set a comms cadence, demanded evidence over hunches, and protected the human while fixing the system. That is incident command: calm is a strategy.

simulations.title: Deploy or rollback?
simulations.brief: The new release is 80% rolled out when the error budget starts burning — but only in one region, and the dashboards are ambiguous. Roll back a mostly-good deploy, or push through on incomplete information?

steps.symptom: Errors climbing in eu-west only. The change looks unrelated to the errors. Rollback takes 20 minutes; the launch event is in an hour.
evidence:
eu-west error rate: 2% -> 9% in 20 min | other regions: flat
Deploy: 80% rolled out | correlation with deploy: unclear
Rollback time: ~20 min | launch event: T-60 min
options: Roll back immediately — errors beat schedules
Hold the rollout (stop at 80%), investigate eu-west for 15 minutes with a hard timebox, then decide
Push to 100% — the errors are probably unrelated
Wait for more data with no timebox
steps.explain: Incomplete information calls for buying information cheaply: freeze the rollout (stop adding risk), timebox the investigation (15 minutes, not 'until we know'), then decide. Instant rollback wastes a maybe-good deploy; pushing through gambles the launch.

steps.symptom: Timebox expired. The eu-west errors are a third-party CDN issue — not your deploy. But the rollback window is closing.
evidence:
eu-west errors: CDN provider incident, confirmed on their status page
Your deploy: clean | Time left before launch: 40 min
options: Roll back anyway — better safe
Resume the rollout to 100% and note the CDN issue in the launch comms
Freeze at 80% through the launch
Blame the CDN publicly
steps.explain: New information updates the decision: the deploy is clean, the culprit is external. You resume — and you communicate the CDN issue proactively so the launch team is not blindsided. Decisions are bets; update them when the odds change.

steps.symptom: Launch succeeded. Now the team wants a rule: 'never deploy before a launch event again.'
evidence: Team: 'Freeze all deploys 48h before any launch.'
options: Approve the freeze — it feels safe
Reject the blanket freeze: this incident was a CDN issue, not a deploy issue. Instead: keep deploys small, keep rollbacks fast, and require a launch-day rollback plan
Extend the freeze to a full week
Let the team vote
steps.explain: Do not legislate against the last incident — legislate against the class of risk. The lesson was not 'deploys are dangerous'; it was 'have a fast rollback and a timeboxed investigation process.' Blanket freezes just move risk around.

simulations.debrief: You bought information instead of gambling, updated the bet when the facts changed, and refused to turn one scare into a permanent bad policy. Decision-making under uncertainty is a skill — you just practiced it.

simulations.title: The blameless postmortem
simulations.brief: Yesterday's outage was caused by an engineer running a command on the wrong host. The postmortem is in an hour. The engineer is dreading it. Run it right.

steps.symptom: The timeline is clear: at 14:02, an engineer ran the production migration against the wrong host. Two hours of downtime.
evidence:
14:02 — migration run against prod instead of staging
14:05 — errors begin | 16:10 — rollback complete
Engineer: 6 months tenure, followed the runbook as written
options: Open the postmortem by naming the engineer and what they did wrong
Open with: 'We are here to understand the system that allowed this, not to judge the person. Walk us through what you saw.'
Skip the postmortem — the cause is obvious
Have the engineer's manager run the session
steps.explain: Blameless is stated out loud, at the start, by the leader — otherwise it is just a word in a doc. 'What did you see?' invites the truth; 'what did you do wrong?' invites defensiveness and silence.

steps.symptom: The engineer explains: the runbook's hostnames differed by one character, and the prompt did not show the environment. Three others admit they nearly did the same.
evidence:
Runbook: hosts 'db-prod-01' vs 'db-prod-01-stg' — one suffix apart
Prompt: no environment indicator | 3 others: 'I almost did that last month'
options: Conclude the engineer should have been more careful
Name the systemic fixes: environment-colored prompts, a confirmation gate on prod migrations, distinct naming — and assign owners and dates
Add 'be more careful' to the runbook
Require two-person approval for every command
steps.explain: Three near-misses mean the system was loaded and waiting for someone. The fixes are environmental (make prod unmistakable, gate destructive actions), owned, and dated. 'Be more careful' is not a fix — it is a wish.

steps.symptom: The postmortem doc is written. An executive asks for 'the name of who caused it' for the board report.
evidence: Exec: 'The board wants accountability. Who was it?'
options: Give the name — the board outranks the process
Refuse and reframe: 'The board gets the systemic causes, the fixes, and the dates. Naming the individual teaches every engineer to hide the next near-miss.'
Give the name but ask them to keep it quiet
Say you do not remember
steps.explain: This is the moment blamelessness is tested — and it is the leader's job to absorb the pressure, not pass it down. The board gets accountability for the system; the individual gets coaching. Trade one for the other and your next postmortem will be fiction.

simulations.debrief: You protected the person, fixed the system, and held the line when accountability theater came knocking. Blameless postmortems are how organizations learn at full speed — because people tell the truth.

simulations.title: The stakeholder ambush
simulations.brief: Mid-incident, two VPs join the bridge and demand an ETA. The team is still diagnosing. Handle the ambush without derailing the response.

steps.symptom: VP Sales: 'Our biggest customer is threatening to churn. When will this be fixed?' VP Eng is silent. The debugger has a promising lead.
evidence:
VP Sales: 'I need a time. The customer is on hold.'
Status: diagnosing, one promising lead, no ETA yet
options: Give an ETA to get them off the bridge — say 30 minutes
Give a process answer, not a time: 'We have a lead and we are testing it now. Next update in 20 minutes. I will come to you — please let the team work.'
Hand the bridge to the VP and step back
Mute the VPs
steps.explain: Never invent an ETA under pressure — a missed invented deadline destroys more trust than no deadline. Give them what you do know (the lead, the next update time) and protect the team's focus. Stakeholders need cadence, not fiction.

steps.symptom: VP Sales again: 'Can we just fail over to the backup? The customer does not care about root cause.'
evidence:
VP Sales: 'Fail over now, investigate later.'
Reality: failover was never tested; backup is 6 hours stale
options: Do the failover — the VP outranks you
Explain the trade honestly: 'Failover is untested and the backup is 6 hours stale — we would trade a fixable outage for data loss. We stay the course unless the lead dies.'
Fail over quietly and hope
Ask the VP to sign off in writing first
steps.explain: Rank does not convert a bad option into a good one. You translate the technical reality into business consequences (data loss vs. outage) and make a recommendation — that is what the IC role is for. Deferring to rank during incidents is how outages get worse.

steps.symptom: Incident resolved. VP Sales apologizes for the pressure. What do you institutionalize?
evidence: VP Sales: 'Sorry — I panicked. How do we do this better next time?'
options: Ban VPs from the bridge
Create a stakeholder protocol: VPs get updates in a separate channel on a fixed cadence, and the IC briefs them — they never join the working bridge uninvited
Accept the apology and change nothing
Make the VP do incident training as punishment
steps.explain: The VP's instinct (protect the customer) was right; the venue was wrong. A stakeholder protocol gives executives what they actually need — timely, honest updates — without injecting pressure into the working team. Design the system for stressed humans.

simulations.debrief: You gave cadence instead of fiction, overruled rank with evidence, and turned an ambush into a protocol. Leadership under pressure is mostly structure plus honesty, repeated.

simulations.title: When the runbook lies
simulations.brief: The runbook says step 4 restarts the service. You ran step 4. The service did not restart — and the runbook has no step 5. Now what?

steps.symptom: Step 4 of the failover runbook: 'Restart the queue service.' You ran it. Nothing happened. The runbook ends at step 4.
evidence:
FAILOVER-07, last updated 14 months ago
Step 4: 'Restart the queue service' — no expected output listed
Reality: command ran, service still down, no step 5
options: Run step 4 again, harder
Stop, verify the service state directly, and check whether the runbook's assumptions still match reality
Declare the runbook useless and improvise the whole failover
Wait for the runbook's author to wake up
steps.explain: When the map and the territory disagree, trust the territory. Verify actual state (is the service down? what does the supervisor say?) before running anything again — repeating a step that silently failed is how you compound outages.

steps.symptom: The service manager shows the queue service as 'failed' — it crashed on a config the runbook never mentions. The config was added 6 months ago.
evidence:
Service: failed (not just stopped)
Cause: unknown config key 'max_batch_v2' — added 6 months ago
Runbook age: 14 months (predates the config)
options: Fix the config and restart — then update the runbook before you forget
Fix the config and restart; update the runbook later
Roll back the config change from 6 months ago
Rebuild the entire service from scratch
steps.explain: Fix the immediate problem, then fix the runbook in the same motion — 'later' never comes, and the next person gets the same lie. The scribe notes both the fix and the doc update while it is fresh.

steps.symptom: Service is up. The team asks: how do we stop runbooks from rotting?
evidence: Team: 'Half our runbooks are stale. What's the fix?'
options: Assign someone to re-read all runbooks quarterly
Make runbooks executable and tested: every runbook gets a drill date, and steps that cannot be run in a drill get flagged. Stale steps are bugs, filed like bugs.
Delete all runbooks and rely on expertise
Write longer, more detailed runbooks
steps.explain: Runbooks rot because nothing tests them. Treat them like code: drills are the tests, stale steps are bugs with owners and due dates. A runbook that has never been drilled is a rumor, not a procedure.

simulations.debrief: You trusted the territory over the map, fixed the doc in the same motion as the system, and turned rot into process. Runbooks are only as good as their last drill.

consoleSims.title: Open the incident ticket
consoleSims.brief: Incident command starts with a paper trail. Open a P1 ticket for the checkout outage, then assign the seeded INC-9001 ticket to yourself as the incident commander.

tasks.instruction: Create a ticket titled 'INC: checkout outage' with priority P1.
tasks.hint: Open New ticket: TITLE='INC: checkout outage', PRIORITY=P1.

tasks.instruction: Assign ticket INC-9001 to m.reyes (the incident commander).
tasks.hint: On the INC-9001 row, assign it: ID=INC-9001, ASSIGNEE=m.reyes.

consoleSims.debrief: Every incident gets a ticket and an owner before anything else. Paper trails are how chaos becomes manageable.

consoleSims.title: Run the incident to resolution
consoleSims.brief: The incident is underway. Move INC-9001 to in-progress, add a status note for the stakeholders, then resolve it when the fix is verified — with a real resolution note.

tasks.instruction: Set ticket INC-9001 status to in-progress.
Add a note to INC-9001: 'IC declared; debug and comms roles assigned.'

params.text: IC declared; debug and comms roles assigned.

tasks.hint: Add a note on INC-9001 with the exact status text.

tasks.instruction: Resolve INC-9001 with resolution 'Rollback verified; monitoring green.'
tasks.hint: Resolve INC-9001 with the exact resolution text.

consoleSims.debrief: In-progress, narrated, resolved with evidence. The ticket is the incident's memory — future you will thank present you.

consoleSims.title: Triage the impossible-travel alert
consoleSims.brief: ALT-101 fired: an impossible-travel login on wkst-042. As IC, make sure it is worked: acknowledge it, assign it to analyst 't.nguyen', and escalate it — authentication anomalies do not wait.

tasks.hint: Click Ack on the ALT-101 row (Impossible travel login).

tasks.instruction: Assign alert ALT-101 to analyst t.nguyen.
tasks.hint: Assign alert form: ALERT ID=ALT-101, ANALYST=t.nguyen.
Click Escalate on the ALT-101 row.

consoleSims.debrief: Acknowledged, owned, escalated. An alert with no owner is just noise with a timestamp.

consoleSims.title: Contain the exfiltration signal
consoleSims.brief: ALT-103: unusual outbound volume from srv-backup-02. Isolate the host to stop potential exfiltration, then create a detection rule 'backup-egress-watch' so the next spike pages someone.

tasks.hint: Click 'Isolate host' on the ALT-103 row.
Open Detection rules: NAME=backup-egress-watch, QUERY describing outbound volume spikes.

consoleSims.debrief: Contain first, detect permanently. Decisive action on ambiguous signals — followed by a rule so the ambiguity shrinks next time.

terminalMissions.title: Who has the conn
terminalMissions.brief: An incident commander first establishes who is present. Print your username.

checks.hint: Run: whoami — who is on the bridge?

terminalMissions.success_message: Presence established. You cannot assign roles to people you have not accounted for.

terminalMissions.title: Name the command post
terminalMissions.brief: Name the machine you are commanding from. Print the hostname.

checks.hint: Run: hostname — name your command post.

terminalMissions.success_message: Command post named. Incidents get locations, not vibes.

terminalMissions.title: Survey the bridge
terminalMissions.brief: Survey your instruments before the crisis. List the home directory.
terminalMissions.success_message: Bridge surveyed. Commanders study the terrain before the battle.

terminalMissions.title: Declare incident command
terminalMissions.brief: The IC for this drill is M. Reyes. Announce it with echo — if nobody says "I am the IC," nobody is.

checks.hint: Run: echo with the declaration (e.g. echo "IC: M. Reyes has command").

terminalMissions.success_message: Command declared. Explicit beats assumed, every time.

terminalMissions.title: Confirm your station
terminalMissions.brief: Print your working directory — a commander knows exactly where they stand.
terminalMissions.success_message: Station confirmed. Clarity of position is clarity of command.

terminalMissions.title: Verify credentials
terminalMissions.brief: Authority must be verifiable. Print your full identity record.
terminalMissions.success_message: Credentials verified. Authority you cannot verify is authority you should not claim.

terminalMissions.title: Sound the all-clear
terminalMissions.brief: The incident is resolved. Announce the all-clear with echo, then print the platform string for the after-action record.

checks.hint: Run: echo with the all-clear (e.g. echo "all-clear, incident resolved").

terminalMissions.success_message: All-clear sounded and recorded. Every incident ends with a clear statement, not a fade-out.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Company facts (verified)
items: Founded 2017 in Orlando, FL — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Philosophy: deny-by-default / default-deny — approve known-good, deny the rest
Customers: 70,000+ organizations, sold heavily through the MSP channel
Funding: $190M Series F, July 2026 (Elephant-led); ~730 employees
Interview address: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando, FL 32810
Culture: in-office 5 days/week; free lunch; post-offer background + drug screening

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

checklist: Sixty-second company brief rehearsed out loud: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone
Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user
“Why ThreatLocker / why cybersecurity” answer tied to prevention and service, not slogans
Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)
Elevation Control answer ready: just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, logged
Triage loop memorized: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
Can you explain supervised vs unsupervised vs anomaly detection with a security example for each?
Can you name three log features you would engineer for a C2 detector and why?
Can you walk through a UEBA alert (baseline, deviation, verification) end to end?
Can you explain the precision/recall tradeoff and how you would set a threshold for a fatigued SOC?
Can you define concept drift and describe a retraining process?
Can you distinguish direct vs indirect prompt injection and jailbreaking?
Can you explain tool poisoning in the MCP ecosystem and three controls against it?
Can you describe insecure output handling and how you would validate agent output?
Can you name the three adversarial ML attack classes and one defense for evasion?
Can you design a SOAR playbook gate: what automates freely, what needs human approval?

media.title: Allowlisting vs blocklisting: default-deny vs default-allow
media.caption: Default-deny stops unknown code without a signature; default-allow runs it until one exists.
media.alt: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, a default-deny gate runs known-good payroll software and denies unknown ransomware with no signature needed; on the right, a default-allow gate runs both until the ransomware is recognized as bad.

media.title: Ringfencing: four leashes on an allowed application
media.caption: Word stays approved, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — while opening its document is allowed.
media.alt: An approved Word application inside a dashed containment ring: arrows show PowerShell launch denied, credential-store registry access denied, external network denied, and document file access allowed.

media.title: The Zero Trust endpoint stack
media.caption: Five deny-by-default layers — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network — watched by Web Control, the Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.
media.alt: A vertical stack of five layers from Allowlisting at the foundation up through Ringfencing, Elevation Control, Storage Control, and Network Control, with side boxes for Web Control, Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and Cyber Hero MDR.

media.title: Application-request triage flow
media.caption: Gather evidence first, then branch: trusted gets a scoped rule, unknown goes to the sandbox, malicious gets a documented deny.
media.alt: Flowchart from request arrival through evidence gathering to a decision diamond branching into three outcomes: approve with a scoped rule, detonate in the Testing Environment then ringfence, or deny with documented evidence.
Diagram of four labeled nodes (user, host, file, domain, IP) joined by labeled directed edges such as logged into, downloaded, and resolved to, illustrating graph vocabulary.
media.caption: Nodes are the things; edges are the relationships. Attackers move along the edges.
media.title: Graph vocabulary: nodes and edges

media.alt: Attack graph with four nodes in a chain: external attacker to VPN gateway to file server to customer database, with a dead-end branch to a printer, showing the shortest path to the crown jewel.
media.caption: The shortest path to the crown jewel is length 3. Break the choke point and the campaign dies.
media.title: Attack graph: shortest path to the crown jewels

media.alt: Seven kill-chain stages as connected graph nodes: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions. Three alerts are annotated at delivery, installation, and command and control.
media.caption: Three 'unrelated' alerts, one kill-chain subgraph. Correlate by shared entities, not by severity.
media.title: Kill chain as a graph

media.alt: A policy engine at the center of a small graph evaluates an access request from a finance user on an untrusted laptop to an R and D code server. The request is denied because there is no prior relationship edge and the device is untrusted.
media.caption: Valid credentials are not enough. The graph checks device trust, history, and relationships on every request.
media.title: Zero Trust runs on relationships
ML detection pipeline: telemetry to triage
media.caption: How raw telemetry becomes scored alerts: features feed the model, the model scores, analysts triage top-down — and analyst verdicts feed retraining.
media.alt: Flow diagram: telemetry sources feed feature extraction, which feeds an ML model, which outputs scored alerts into an analyst triage queue, with a feedback arrow for retraining.

media.title: UEBA: baseline vs deviation
media.caption: UEBA learns each user's normal hours, locations, and volumes, then scores deviations from that baseline.
media.alt: 24-hour timeline showing a shaded normal login window from 8 AM to 6 PM with normal logins inside it, and a red anomaly marker at 2:47 AM for a foreign login scoring 97 out of 100.

media.title: Indirect prompt injection attack flow
media.caption: An attacker hides instructions in data the agent retrieves; the agent mistakes data for instructions and misuses its tools.
media.alt: Attack flow diagram: hidden instruction in an email is read by an AI agent, which mistakes it for a command and calls a privileged tool, causing fraud; three defense boxes below: sanitize content, least-privilege tools, human approval.
